title: Der Hund und der Sperling
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 58. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, Wuth und todt).
about: KHM 58, a revenge tale told with the level cheerfulness of a fable. A sparrow befriends a starving sheepdog and feeds him off the town’s shop-boards; when a carter drives over the sleeping dog out of sheer obstinacy, the sparrow answers with a patient, escalating ruin — the wine, the three horses, the grain in the loft, the furniture, and at last the man himself. Nothing here is softened, least of all the ending. Spelling follows the 1857 edition, so you will meet older forms such as gieng, todt, daß, Waizen and Wuth.

sentences.t: Ein Schäferhund hatte keinen guten Herrn, sondern einen, der ihn Hunger leiden ließ.
sentences.l: A shepherd-dog had no good master, but rather one who let him suffer hunger.
sentences.i: A sheepdog had no good master, but one who left him to go hungry.
sentences.n: “jemanden Hunger leiden lassen” — to let someone suffer hunger, i.e. to keep him starved.

sentences.t: Wie ers nicht länger bei ihm aushalten konnte, gieng er ganz traurig fort.
sentences.l: As he could no longer hold out with him, he went away quite sorrowful.
sentences.i: Since he could bear it with him no longer, he went off, thoroughly downcast.
sentences.n: wie here means “as, since” rather than “how.” ers = er es.

sentences.t: Auf der Straße begegnete ihm ein Sperling, der sprach „Bruder Hund, warum bist du so traurig?“
sentences.l: On the road there met him a sparrow, who spoke “brother dog, why are you so sad?”
sentences.i: On the road a sparrow met him and said: “Brother Dog, why are you so sad?”
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative — in German one “meets to” a person (begegnete ihm).

sentences.t: Antwortete der Hund „ich bin hungrig, und habe nichts zu fressen.“
sentences.l: Answered the dog “I am hungry, and have nothing to eat.”
sentences.i: The dog answered: “I am hungry, and have nothing to eat.”
sentences.n: fressen is the verb for an animal feeding; essen belongs to people. The tale keeps fressen for the dog throughout.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Sperling „lieber Bruder, komm mit in die Stadt, so will ich dich satt machen.“
sentences.l: Then spoke the sparrow “dear brother, come along into the town, then will I make you full.”
sentences.i: Then the sparrow said: “Dear brother, come with me into the town, and I will see you fed.”
sentences.n: “satt machen” = to make full, to feed until one has had enough; satt is the word for that state, and it runs through the whole first half of the tale.

sentences.t: Also giengen sie zusammen in die Stadt, und als sie vor einen Fleischerladen kamen, sprach der Sperling zum Hunde „da bleib stehen, ich will dir ein Stück Fleisch herunter picken,“ setzte sich auf den Laden, schaute sich um, ob ihn auch niemand bemerkte, und pickte, zog und zerrte so lang an einem Stück, das am Rande lag, bis es herunter rutschte.
sentences.l: So they went together into the town, and when they came before a butcher’s-shop, the sparrow spoke to the dog “stay standing there, I will peck a piece of meat down for you,” set himself on the shop-board, looked himself around whether nobody was noticing him, and pecked, pulled and tugged so long at a piece that lay at the edge, until it slid down.
sentences.i: So they went into the town together; and when they came to a butcher’s shop, the sparrow said to the dog: “Stand there, and I will peck a piece of meat down for you.” He settled on the shop-board, looked about to see whether anyone was watching him, and pecked and pulled and tugged at a piece lying on the edge until it slipped down.
sentences.n: Laden here is the open stall or shop-board, which is why a bird can sit on it. “bleib stehen” = stay standing, i.e. wait there.

sentences.t: Da packte es der Hund, lief in eine Ecke und fraß es auf.
sentences.l: Then the dog seized it, ran into a corner and ate it up.

sentences.t: Sprach der Sperling „nun komm mit zu einem andern Laden, da will ich dir noch ein Stück herunter holen, damit du satt wirst.“
sentences.l: Spoke the sparrow “now come along to another shop, there will I fetch you down another piece, so that you become full.”
sentences.i: Said the sparrow: “Now come along to another shop, and I will fetch you down another piece, so that you have your fill.”

sentences.t: Als der Hund auch das zweite Stück gefressen hatte, fragte der Sperling „Bruder Hund, bist du nun satt?“
sentences.l: When the dog had eaten the second piece too, the sparrow asked “brother dog, are you full now?”

sentences.t: „Ja, Fleisch bin ich satt,“ antwortete er, „aber ich habe noch kein Brot gekriegt.“
sentences.l: “Yes, meat I am full of,” answered he, “but I have got no bread yet.”
sentences.i: “Yes, of meat I have had my fill,” he answered, “but I have had no bread yet.”
sentences.n: Fleisch stands first as the thing he has had enough of — “as far as meat goes, I am full.” kriegen is the everyday word for “to get.”

sentences.t: Sprach der Sperling „das sollst du auch haben, komm nur mit.“
sentences.l: Spoke the sparrow “that shall you have too, just come along.”
sentences.i: Said the sparrow: “That you shall have as well — only come along.”

sentences.t: Da führte er ihn an einen Beckerladen und pickte an ein paar Brötchen, bis sie herunter rollten, und als der Hund noch mehr wollte, führte er ihn zu einem andern und holte ihm noch einmal Brot herab.
sentences.l: Then he led him to a baker’s-shop and pecked at a couple of little-loaves, until they rolled down, and when the dog wanted still more, he led him to another and fetched bread down for him once again.
sentences.i: Then he led him to a baker’s shop and pecked at a couple of rolls until they rolled down; and when the dog wanted still more, he led him to another and fetched him down bread a second time.
sentences.n: Beckerladen — the 1857 text writes Becker for modern Bäcker. Brötchen is the diminutive of Brot, a small loaf or roll.

sentences.t: Wie das verzehrt war, sprach der Sperling „Bruder Hund, bist du nun satt?“
sentences.l: When that was consumed, the sparrow spoke “brother dog, are you full now?”

sentences.t: „Ja,“ antwortete er, „nun wollen wir ein bischen vor die Stadt gehen.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” answered he, “now we will go a little bit out before the town.”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he answered, “now let us go a little way out of the town.”
sentences.n: “vor die Stadt” = out in front of the town, beyond the gate. bischen is the 1857 spelling of bisschen.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie beide hinaus auf die Landstraße.
sentences.l: Then they both went out onto the highroad.

sentences.t: Es war aber warmes Wetter, und als sie ein Eckchen gegangen waren, sprach der Hund „ich bin müde und möchte gerne schlafen.“
sentences.l: But it was warm weather, and when they had gone a little-corner, the dog spoke “I am tired and would gladly sleep.”
sentences.i: But the weather was warm, and when they had gone a short stretch, the dog said: “I am tired and would gladly sleep.”
sentences.n: “ein Eckchen” (a little corner) is colloquial for a short distance.

sentences.t: „Ja, schlaf nur,“ antwortete der Sperling, „ich will mich derweil auf einen Zweig setzen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, just sleep,” answered the sparrow, “I will set myself meanwhile on a branch.”
sentences.i: “Yes, sleep away,” answered the sparrow. “I will perch on a branch in the meantime.”

sentences.t: Der Hund legte sich also auf die Straße und schlief fest ein.
sentences.l: So the dog laid himself on the road and fell fast asleep.

sentences.t: Während er da lag und schlief, kam ein Fuhrmann heran gefahren, der hatte einen Wagen mit drei Pferden, und hatte zwei Fässer Wein geladen.
sentences.l: While he lay there and slept, a carter came driving up, he had a wagon with three horses, and had two casks of wine loaded.
sentences.i: While he lay there sleeping, a carter came driving up; he had a wagon and three horses, and two casks of wine loaded on it.
sentences.n: Fuhrmann — a carter, a man who hauls goods by wagon for hire; his horses and cart are his livelihood, which is what makes the sparrow’s threat serious.

sentences.t: Der Sperling aber sah daß er nicht ausbiegen wollte, sondern in der Fahrgleise blieb, in welcher der Hund lag, da rief er „Fuhrmann, thus nicht, oder ich mache dich arm.“
sentences.l: But the sparrow saw that he would not turn aside, but rather stayed in the wheel-rut in which the dog lay, then he called “carter, do it not, or I will make you poor.”
sentences.i: But the sparrow saw that he would not turn aside, but kept to the rut in which the dog lay; so he called out: “Carter, do not do it, or I will make you poor.”
sentences.n: thus = thu es (modern tu es), “do it.” Fahrgleise is the rut worn into an unpaved road by wheels.

sentences.t: Der Fuhrmann aber brummte vor sich „du wirst mich nicht arm machen,“ knallte mit der Peitsche und trieb den Wagen über den Hund, daß ihn die Räder todt fuhren.
sentences.l: But the carter growled before himself “you will not make me poor,” cracked with the whip and drove the wagon over the dog, so that the wheels ran him dead.
sentences.i: But the carter muttered to himself, “You will not make me poor,” cracked his whip and drove the wagon over the dog, so that the wheels crushed him dead.
sentences.n: “todt fahren” — to run over and kill. German builds such pairs freely: todt schlagen, to strike dead. todt is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: Da rief der Sperling „du hast mir meinen Bruder Hund todt gefahren, das soll dich Karre und Gaul kosten.“
sentences.l: Then called the sparrow “you have driven my brother dog dead on me, that shall cost you cart and nag.”
sentences.i: Then the sparrow cried: “You have driven over my brother dog and killed him; it shall cost you cart and horse.”
sentences.n: mir is a dative of loss — the dog was killed to the sparrow’s cost. Gaul is a plain, rough word for a workhorse, closer to “nag” than to Pferd.

sentences.t: „Ja, Karre und Gaul,“ sagte der Fuhrmann, „was könntest du mir schaden!“ und fuhr weiter.
sentences.l: “Yes, cart and nag,” said the carter, “what harm could you do me!” and drove on.

sentences.t: Da kroch der Sperling unter das Wagentuch und pickte an dem einen Spuntloch so lange, bis er den Spunt losbrachte: da lief der ganze Wein heraus, ohne daß es der Fuhrmann merkte.
sentences.l: Then the sparrow crept under the wagon-cloth and pecked at the one bung-hole so long, until he broke the bung loose: then all the wine ran out, without the carter noticing it.
sentences.i: Then the sparrow crept under the wagon-cloth and pecked at the one bung-hole until he worked the bung loose; and out ran all the wine, without the carter noticing.
sentences.n: Spunt (modern Spund) is the wooden plug closing a cask; the Spuntloch is the hole it sits in.

sentences.t: Und als er einmal hinter sich blickte, sah er daß der Wagen tröpfelte, untersuchte die Fässer und fand daß eins leer war.
sentences.l: And when he once glanced behind himself, he saw that the wagon was dripping, examined the casks and found that one was empty.

sentences.t: „Ach, ich armer Mann!“ rief er.
sentences.l: “Ah, I poor man!” called he.
sentences.i: “Alas, poor man that I am!” he cried.
sentences.n: “ich armer Mann” — an exclamation of self-pity, and the refrain the whole tale is built on; the sparrow answers it five more times.

sentences.t: „Noch nicht arm genug“ sprach der Sperling und flog dem einen Pferd auf den Kopf und pickte ihm die Augen aus.
sentences.l: “Not poor enough yet,” spoke the sparrow and flew onto the one horse’s head and pecked its eyes out.
sentences.i: “Not poor enough yet,” said the sparrow, and flew onto the head of one of the horses and pecked its eyes out.
sentences.n: “pickte ihm die Augen aus” — the possessor sits in the dative (ihm): pecked the eyes out on it.

sentences.t: Als der Fuhrmann das sah, zog er seine Hacke heraus und wollte den Sperling treffen, aber der Sperling flog in die Höhe, und der Fuhrmann traf seinen Gaul auf den Kopf, daß er todt hinfiel.
sentences.l: When the carter saw that, he drew his axe out and wanted to hit the sparrow, but the sparrow flew into the height, and the carter struck his nag on the head, so that it fell down dead.
sentences.i: When the carter saw that, he pulled out his axe to strike the sparrow; but the sparrow flew up into the air, and the carter caught his own horse on the head, so that it dropped dead.
sentences.n: Hacke is the chopping or digging tool carried on the wagon — an axe or a mattock; the tale never says which. “in die Höhe” = up into the air.

sentences.t: „Ach, ich armer Mann!“ rief er.
sentences.l: “Ah, I poor man!” called he.
sentences.i: “Alas, poor man that I am!” he cried.

sentences.t: „Noch nicht arm genug“ sprach der Sperling, und als der Fuhrmann mit den zwei Pferden weiter fuhr, kroch der Sperling wieder unter das Tuch und pickte den Spunt auch am zweiten Faß los, daß aller Wein herausschwankte.
sentences.l: “Not poor enough yet,” spoke the sparrow, and when the carter drove on with the two horses, the sparrow crept again under the cloth and pecked the bung loose on the second cask too, so that all the wine surged out.
sentences.i: “Not poor enough yet,” said the sparrow; and when the carter drove on with his two horses, the sparrow crept under the cloth again and worked the bung loose on the second cask as well, so that all that wine slopped out too.
sentences.n: herausschwanken — to slosh or surge out; the wine heaves out with the rocking of the wagon.

sentences.t: Als es der Fuhrmann gewahr wurde, rief er wieder, „ach, ich armer Mann!“ aber der Sperling antwortete „noch nicht arm genug,“ setzte sich dem zweiten Pferd auf den Kopf und pickte ihm die Augen aus.
sentences.l: When the carter became aware of it, he called again, “ah, I poor man!” but the sparrow answered “not poor enough yet,” set himself on the second horse’s head and pecked its eyes out.
sentences.i: When the carter grew aware of it he cried again, “Alas, poor man that I am!” But the sparrow answered, “Not poor enough yet,” settled on the second horse’s head, and pecked its eyes out.
sentences.n: “gewahr werden” = to become aware of, to catch sight of — an elevated older phrase.

sentences.t: Der Fuhrmann lief herbei und holte mit seiner Hacke aus, aber der Sperling flog in die Höhe: da traf der Schlag, das Pferd daß es hinfiel.
sentences.l: The carter ran up and swung out with his axe, but the sparrow flew into the height: then the blow struck the horse, so that it fell down.
sentences.i: The carter ran up and swung his axe, but the sparrow flew up into the air — and the blow caught the horse, so that it fell.
sentences.n: “ausholen” = to draw the arm back for a stroke. The 1857 comma after “der Schlag” sits where a modern text would put none; the sense is that the blow landed on the horse.

sentences.t: „Ach, ich armer Mann!“
sentences.l: “Ah, I poor man!”
sentences.i: “Alas, poor man that I am!”

sentences.t: „Noch nicht arm genug“ sprach der Sperling, setzte sich auch dem dritten Pferd auf den Kopf und pickte ihm nach den Augen.
sentences.l: “Not poor enough yet,” spoke the sparrow, set himself on the third horse’s head too and pecked at its eyes.
sentences.i: “Not poor enough yet,” said the sparrow, and settled on the third horse’s head as well, and pecked at its eyes.
sentences.n: “nach etwas picken” = to peck at something, aiming for it — this time we are not told he succeeds.

sentences.t: Der Fuhrmann schlug in seinem Zorn, ohne umzusehen, auf den Sperling los, traf ihn aber nicht, sondern schlug auch sein drittes Pferd todt.
sentences.l: The carter struck in his rage, without looking around, out at the sparrow, but did not hit him, but rather struck his third horse dead too.
sentences.i: In his rage the carter struck out at the sparrow without looking, and missed him, and struck his third horse dead as well.
sentences.n: “auf etwas losschlagen” = to lay into something. “ohne umzusehen” — without looking round to see what he is hitting.

sentences.t: „Ach, ich armer Mann!“ rief er.
sentences.l: “Ah, I poor man!” called he.
sentences.i: “Alas, poor man that I am!” he cried.

sentences.t: „Noch nicht arm genug,“ antwortete der Sperling, „jetzt will ich dich daheim arm machen,“ und flog fort.
sentences.l: “Not poor enough yet,” answered the sparrow, “now I will make you poor at home,” and flew away.

sentences.t: Der Fuhrmann mußte den Wagen stehen lassen, und gieng voll Zorn und Ärger heim.
sentences.l: The carter had to leave the wagon standing, and went home full of rage and vexation.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach er zu seiner Frau, „was hab ich Unglück gehabt! der Wein ist ausgelaufen, und die Pferde sind alle drei todt.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” spoke he to his wife, “what misfortune have I had! the wine has run out, and the horses are all three dead.”
sentences.i: “Oh,” he said to his wife, “what ill luck I have had! The wine has all run out, and the horses are dead, all three.”

sentences.t: „Ach, Mann,“ antwortete sie, „was für ein böser Vogel ist ins Haus gekommen! er hat alle Vögel auf der Welt zusammen gebracht, und die sind droben über unsern Waizen hergefallen und fressen ihn auf.“
sentences.l: “Ah, husband,” answered she, “what a wicked bird has come into the house! he has brought together all the birds in the world, and they have fallen upon our wheat up there and are eating it up.”
sentences.i: “Oh, husband,” she answered, “what a wicked bird has got into the house! He has gathered every bird in the world, and they have fallen on our wheat up above and are eating it up.”
sentences.n: Mann is “husband” when a wife says it. “über etwas herfallen” = to fall upon, to descend on. Waizen is the 1857 spelling of Weizen.

sentences.t: Da stieg er hinauf, und tausend und tausend Vögel saßen auf dem Boden, und hatten den Waizen aufgefressen, und der Sperling saß mitten darunter.
sentences.l: Then he climbed up, and thousand and thousand birds sat on the loft-floor, and had eaten the wheat up, and the sparrow sat in the middle among them.
sentences.i: So he climbed up; and a thousand upon a thousand birds were sitting on the loft floor, and had eaten the wheat up, and the sparrow sat in the midst of them.
sentences.n: Boden here is the loft under the roof, where grain was stored — not the ground. darunter = among them.

sentences.t: Da rief der Fuhrmann „ach, ich armer Mann!“
sentences.l: Then called the carter “ah, I poor man!”
sentences.i: Then the carter cried: “Alas, poor man that I am!”

sentences.t: „Noch nicht arm genug,“ antwortete der Sperling, „Fuhrmann, es kostet dir noch dein Leben,“ und flog hinaus.
sentences.l: “Not poor enough yet,” answered the sparrow, “carter, it will cost you your life besides,” and flew out.
sentences.i: “Not poor enough yet,” answered the sparrow. “Carter, it will cost you your life as well” — and flew out.
sentences.n: kosten normally takes the accusative (dich); the tale uses the dative dir, an older and regional usage. It returns as the sparrow’s refrain to the end.

sentences.t: Da hatte der Fuhrmann all sein Gut verloren, gieng hinab in die Stube, setzte sich hinter den Ofen und zwar ganz bös und giftig.
sentences.l: Now the carter had lost all his goods, went down into the parlour, set himself behind the stove and that quite cross and venomous.
sentences.i: Now the carter had lost everything he owned; he went down into the parlour and sat down behind the stove, and in a black and poisonous humour.
sentences.n: “hinter den Ofen” — the warm nook behind the tiled stove, the household’s sulking-place. “und zwar” tacks on an emphatic specification: “and that, mind you…”

sentences.t: Der Sperling aber saß draußen vor dem Fenster und rief „Fuhrmann, es kostet dir dein Leben.“
sentences.l: But the sparrow sat outside before the window and called “carter, it will cost you your life.”

sentences.t: Da griff der Fuhrmann die Hacke und warf sie nach dem Sperling: aber er schlug nur die Fensterscheiben entzwei und traf den Vogel nicht.
sentences.l: Then the carter grasped the axe and threw it at the sparrow: but he struck only the window-panes in two and did not hit the bird.
sentences.i: Then the carter snatched up the axe and threw it at the sparrow; but he only smashed the window-panes and did not hit the bird.
sentences.n: entzwei = in two, to pieces; “entzwei schlagen” = to smash.

sentences.t: Der Sperling hüpfte nun herein, setzte sich auf den Ofen und rief „Fuhrmann, es kostet dir dein Leben.“
sentences.l: The sparrow now hopped in, set himself on the stove and called “carter, it will cost you your life.”

sentences.t: Dieser, ganz toll und blind vor Wuth, schlägt den Ofen entzwei, und so fort, wie der Sperling von einem Ort zum andern fliegt, sein ganzes Hausgeräth, Spieglein, Bänke, Tisch, und zuletzt die Wände seines Hauses, und kann ihn nicht treffen.
sentences.l: This one, quite mad and blind with fury, smashes the stove in two, and so on, as the sparrow flies from one place to the other, his whole household-gear, little-mirrors, benches, table, and at last the walls of his house, and cannot hit him.
sentences.i: The man, crazed and blind with fury, smashes the stove to pieces, and so on — as the sparrow flies from one place to the next — all his household stuff, the little mirrors, the benches, the table, and at last the very walls of his house; and still cannot hit him.
sentences.n: The telling slips into the present tense here and mostly keeps it to the last line, though past forms (erwischte, streckte) still turn up alongside — the frenzy told as though it were happening now. Dieser (“this one”) picks up the carter. vor here means “from, out of” a cause: blind with rage.

sentences.t: Endlich aber erwischte er ihn doch mit der Hand.
sentences.l: But at last he caught him after all with his hand.
sentences.i: At last, though, he did catch him with his hand.

sentences.t: Da sprach seine Frau „soll ich ihn todt schlagen?“
sentences.l: Then spoke his wife “shall I strike him dead?”
sentences.i: Then his wife said: “Shall I strike him dead?”

sentences.t: „Nein,“ rief er, „das wäre zu gelind, der soll viel mörderlicher sterben, ich will ihn verschlingen,“ und nimmt ihn, und verschlingt ihn auf einmal.
sentences.l: “No,” called he, “that would be too mild, that one shall die much more murderously, I will swallow him,” and takes him, and swallows him at one go.
sentences.i: “No,” he cried, “that would be too gentle; he shall die far more murderously — I will swallow him,” and he takes him and swallows him down at a gulp.
sentences.n: gelind (modern gelinde) = mild, gentle. mörderlicher — “more murderously,” a comparative built off Mörder, murderer.

sentences.t: Der Sperling aber fängt an in seinem Leibe zu flattern, flattert wieder herauf, dem Mann in den Mund: da streckte er den Kopf heraus und ruft „Fuhrmann, es kostet dir doch dein Leben.“
sentences.l: But the sparrow begins to flutter in his body, flutters up again, into the man’s mouth: then he stretched his head out and calls “carter, it will cost you your life after all.”
sentences.i: But the sparrow begins to flutter inside his body, flutters up again into the man’s mouth; then he put his head out and calls: “Carter, it will cost you your life after all.”
sentences.n: Leib is the body, here the belly. “dem Mann in den Mund” — the person in the dative, the destination in the accusative. doch = after all, in spite of everything.

sentences.t: Der Fuhrmann reicht seiner Frau die Hacke und spricht „Frau, schlag mir den Vogel im Munde todt.“
sentences.l: The carter hands his wife the axe and says “wife, strike me the bird dead in the mouth.”
sentences.i: The carter hands his wife the axe and says: “Wife, strike the bird dead in my mouth.”
sentences.n: mir is an ethical dative — “for me,” marking whose business this is; English cannot really carry it. It also points the blow, fatally, at his own head.

sentences.t: Die Frau schlägt zu, schlägt aber fehl, und schlägt dem Fuhrmann gerade auf den Kopf, so daß er todt hinfällt.
sentences.l: The wife strikes, but strikes amiss, and strikes the carter straight on the head, so that he falls down dead.
sentences.i: The wife strikes — and strikes amiss, and catches the carter square on the head, so that he falls down dead.

sentences.t: Der Sperling aber fliegt auf und davon.
sentences.l: But the sparrow flies up and away.
sentences.n: “auf und davon” = up and off, gone for good — a set phrase, and the last word of the tale.
